title: Engineering Projects
text:
This website is a collection of engineering projects, home projects, calculations, and analysis. I would like to build out a site where I can access common technical knowledge. In my line of work, diverse technical projects tend to be lumped into handfuls of months or years as projects shift around. Recently I find myself digging up project work from 5-10 years prior, and trying to remember why we made the decisiosn at the time.
Times are changing and AI tools will soon (can already) do everything I intend to document on this site, but it will be nice to have a fixed set of data analyzed and verified that I can come back to wihtout wondering whether or not AI crapped itself or picked a random number in the middle of an analysis, which is still common. AI can do a lot of things extremely well where accuracy is not important, but for experimental sciences this couldn’t be further from the truth. That being said, I use AI for a lot of tasking now. No more looking at help files, no more coding from scratch, CAD and CNC programming are next on the list to get overtaken by AI efficiency. As scary as AI can be portrayed, I’m actually excited to have it take over all of the low-level operations of day to day technical/engineering work. The real challenge down the road will be how people can mentally manage all of the additional work and diversity of knowledge that AI will enable.

title: Charcoal BBQ Controller
text: Once upon a time I got tired of tweaking my bbq dampers very hour for long smokes of brisket or pork shoulder. I put together an Arduino based PID fan controller that provided air flow from the bottom of the bbq, and I closed down the top damper. One challenge with this setup was reading out the temperature from a thermistor since I didn’t want to buy a thermocouple amplifier just for this project.

title: Charcoal BBQ Controller
text:
Thermistor calibration
To calibrate the thermistor I filled a small pot with oil, and used a thermapen (food thermometer) and Fluke K type thermocouple as reference thermometers. I turned the burner on the lowest setting, continuously stirred the oil and moved the three thermometers (thermistor = unknown, thermapen, thermocouple) continuously to get an average of the oil bath temperature. The data and fit curve used are shown below:
\[1/T = (a + b \cdot log(R) + c \cdot (log(R))^3)\]
*all units are converted to Kelvin and Ohms before fitting.
This fit curve was uesd in the Arduino to calculate the temperature of the thermistor probes.


Code
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.optimize import curve_fit

# 1. Define fit curve function here
def custom_curve(x, a, b, c):
    """
    Change this mathematical formula to match the curve you want to fit.
    Currently set to a quadratic function: y = 1/(a+b*np.log(x)+c*(np.log(x))**3)
    """
    return (a+b*np.log(x)+c*(np.log(x))**3)

# 2. Read the CSV file
df = pd.read_csv("Thermistor-Oil.csv")

# Extract the X and Y columns
T_data = (df["BGE temp (F)"].values-32)*(5/9)+273.15
R_data = df["Thermistor (kOhm)"].values*1000
R_error = 0.005*R_data + 1000
T_error = 1

# 3. Fit the curve to the data
# curve_fit returns:
#   popt: Optimized parameters (a, b, c)
#   pcov: Covariance matrix (used to calculate parameter errors)
p0_guess = [1.1e-3, 2.3e-4, 8.7e-8]
bounds = (0, [1e-1, 1e-2, 1e-5]) 

popt, pcov = curve_fit(custom_curve, R_data, 1./T_data, p0=p0_guess, bounds=bounds)

# Print the fitted parameters
print("Fitted parameters:")
print(f"a = {popt[0]}")
print(f"b = {popt[1]}")
print(f"c = {popt[2]}")

#a = 0.002240733
#b = 0.000350373
#c = 0.000021379

# 4. (Optional) Plot the original data and the fitted curve
# plt.scatter(T_data, R_data, color="red", label="Data")
plt.errorbar(T_data, R_data/1000, yerr=R_error/1000, xerr=T_error, fmt='o', color="red", label="Data", ms=2, capsize=4)

# Generate smooth X values for the curve line
R_fit = np.linspace(min(R_data), max(R_data), 100)
T_fit = 1./custom_curve(R_fit, *popt)  # *popt unpacks the optimized a, b, c

plt.plot(T_fit, R_fit/1000, color="blue", label="Fitted Curve")
plt.xlabel("Temperature (K)")
plt.ylabel("Resistance (kOhm)")
plt.legend()
plt.show()


Fitted parameters:
a = 0.0006879104473030154
b = 0.00017389502714043695
c = 1.0273748450819405e-07

title: Charcoal BBQ Controller
text:
BBQ Setup
The second part of this setup was programming the Arduino with PID control which is pretty straight forward. Then the control box needed to be built with a fan, which is shown below. The fan is trapped in a compartment on the left side of the box to transition from the fan to the tubing. The intake to the fan is on the external side of the box. The display in the box is for realtime temperature and fan speed control readout, and the second board in addition to the arduino is a motor controller board to provide the higher currents that the motor needs.

title: Charcoal BBQ Controller
text:
BBQ In Action!
The image below shows the BBQ output and stability. The setpoint for the first portion of the cook was 225F and then it was increased to 300F after 9.75 hours. The black data is the grill temperature, the blue is the food probe, and the red is the fan percentage of power. The fan power is shifted on the plot to be between 100 and 200.
It took a couple of runs to get the PID parameters tuned, but ulitimately was quite stable meaning I no longer had to baby-sit the bbq for long cooks.

In the data above I am using pulse width modulated motor control for the fan, but ran into issues with the facn being oversized and for many runs the PWM signal was so small that the fan wouldn’t even spin up. To overcome this, I switched to ON/OFF control with an integration window. I implemented this by converting the PWM signal to a fan run time signal in a 5 or 10 second window. So a 10% PWM signal in a 10 second window means the fan would turn on for 1 second and turn off for the remaining 9 seconds. This worked very well, but ultimately killed the fan because of the constant inrush current needed to start the fan every 5-10 seconds.
While hunting for a smaller fan a few years later I noticed the SMOBOT controller. From a longevity perspective this is much better design than the active fan control I had implemented. This new controller also allowed for remote internet connections so I could get feedback from the BBQ while away from the house. This SMOBOT controller has worked so well over the last 7 years that I finally disassembled the Arduino model I made.
